question_blueprint.correct_answer_concept: A smaller molecule capable of hydrogen bonding can have a higher boiling point than a somewhat heavier similar molecule that cannot hydrogen-bond, because hydrogen bonding can outweigh the mass-based increase in dispersion forces.
question_blueprint.expected_reasoning: Students should compare two structurally similar molecules with close molar masses, identify whether each pure substance can form intermolecular hydrogen bonds, and recognize that boiling point depends on the strongest overall intermolecular attractions present in the liquid. They should conclude that the molecule with an O-H or N-H bond has stronger intermolecular attraction and therefore the higher boiling point, despite not necessarily having the larger molar mass.
question_blueprint.question_style_notes: Use a comparison such as propan-1-ol versus propanal or ethanal versus ethane-1,2-like alternatives with one clearly hydrogen-bonding substance and one slightly heavier non-hydrogen-bonding substance. Ask which has the higher boiling point and why. Include distractors that reflect the heavier-mass-always-higher idea, confusion between bond polarity and hydrogen bonding, and covalent-bond-strength reasoning. Avoid repeating ethanol vs dimethyl ether or any already used pairings.

last_candidate.question: Which compound has the higher boiling point, pentane or 2-methylbutane, and what is the best explanation for the difference?

options.A: Pentane, because its less-branched shape gives a larger surface area and stronger dispersion forces between molecules.
options.B: 2-Methylbutane, because branching increases the number of intermolecular contacts and strengthens dispersion forces.
options.C: Pentane, because it contains stronger covalent bonds, so more energy is needed for the liquid to boil.
options.D: 2-Methylbutane, because both substances are nonpolar and therefore must have the same boiling point unless one can hydrogen-bond.

last_candidate.explanation: Pentane and 2-methylbutane are isomers with the same molar mass, so the boiling-point difference is not due to mass. Both are nonpolar, so the main intermolecular force in each is London dispersion. Pentane is less branched and has a more extended shape, which gives greater surface contact between molecules and stronger dispersion forces. Stronger intermolecular attractions lead to a higher boiling point, so pentane boils at a higher temperature than 2-methylbutane.
